description: Algorithms that sit beside the main branches: number theory (Euclid, sieves, modular arithmetic), the fast Fourier transform, more string search, streaming and sketching, and computational geometry.

concepts.title: Modular Arithmetic
concepts.summary: Arithmetic on a clock: numbers wrap around after reaching a modulus. It underlies checksums, hashing, calendars, and nearly all of public-key cryptography, where enormous numbers are combined and only the remainder is kept.

concepts.title: Euclid's Algorithm
concepts.summary: The oldest algorithm still in use: to find the greatest common divisor, replace the larger number by its remainder on division by the smaller, and repeat. Over 2,300 years old, and the engine of modular inverses and RSA.

concepts.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
concepts.summary: Find all primes up to n by crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn. What remains is prime. About 2,200 years old, it is still the fastest simple way to list primes, and a template for the sieve methods of number theory.

concepts.title: Fast Exponentiation
concepts.summary: Compute aᵇ mod m by repeated squaring, in about log b steps, never letting the numbers grow. It is what makes RSA and Diffie–Hellman practical: raising a 2,048-bit number to a 2,048-bit power takes microseconds.

concepts.title: Fast Fourier Transform
concepts.summary: A way to compute the Fourier transform in n log n steps instead of n². Rediscovered by Cooley and Tukey in 1965, it turned spectral analysis from a supercomputer job into an everyday tool, and it sits inside audio, images, radio, and fast multiplication.

concepts.title: Rabin–Karp
concepts.summary: Search for a pattern by comparing fingerprints: a rolling hash of each window of the text is updated in constant time as the window slides. It finds many patterns at once and underlies plagiarism detectors.

concepts.title: Boyer–Moore
concepts.summary: Compare the pattern from its end, and on a mismatch skip ahead by as much as the mismatched character allows. It often examines only a fraction of the text, which is why the search in most editors and in grep is this or a cousin.

concepts.title: Suffix Arrays
concepts.summary: Sort all the suffixes of a text and any substring query becomes a binary search. It is the compact cousin of the suffix tree and the basis of genome indexing, where a text of billions of letters must be searched again and again.

concepts.title: Streaming Algorithms
concepts.summary: Algorithms that see each item once and remember almost nothing: count distinct users, find frequent items, or sample uniformly from a stream too large to store. They trade a small, controlled error for memory measured in kilobytes.

concepts.title: HyperLogLog
concepts.summary: Estimate how many distinct items are in a huge stream using a few kilobytes: hash each item, and track the longest run of leading zeros seen. Rare patterns imply many items. Redis and BigQuery use it to count billions of users to within a percent or two.

concepts.title: Count–Min Sketch
concepts.summary: Estimate how often each item occurs in a stream using a small table of counters and several hash functions. It never undercounts and overcounts only slightly. It finds heavy hitters in network traffic, trending topics, and query logs.

concepts.title: Reservoir Sampling
concepts.summary: Pick a uniformly random sample of k items from a stream of unknown length, keeping only k in memory. Each new item replaces a random earlier one with just the right probability. Simple, exact, and used for sampling logs and datasets.

concepts.title: Computational Geometry
concepts.summary: Algorithms for shapes: finding the outline of a scatter of points, the closest pair, whether two polygons overlap. It powers maps, collision detection in games, CAD, and robotics.

concepts.title: Convex Hulls
concepts.summary: The smallest convex shape enclosing a set of points: a rubber band snapped around pins on a board. It can be found in n log n time and is a building block for collision detection, outlier detection, and shape analysis.

concepts.title: Closest Pair
concepts.summary: Find the two nearest points among n without comparing every pair. Divide and conquer gets it in n log n, a textbook example of how a smart split beats brute force.
